layers.title: People per km² (modelled)
layers.note: HYDE spreads each country's estimated population over the land by models of where people lived (soils, climate, distance to water and towns); a picture of the estimates, not a census map. Before about 1800 it rests on few figures.

source.citation: Klein Goldewijk, K., Beusen, A., Doelman, J., Stehfest, E. (2017) Anthropogenic land use estimates for the Holocene – HYDE 3.2. Earth System Science Data 9:927–953, doi:10.5194/essd-9-927-2017. Data: HYDE 3.2.1 baseline, DANS, doi:10.17026/dans-25g-gez3

layers.title: Cropland (modelled)
layers.note: Arable land as a share of each cell, from HYDE's country estimates spread by soil suitability and population; pasture and grazing are not included.

source.citation: Klein Goldewijk, K., Beusen, A., Doelman, J., Stehfest, E. (2017) Anthropogenic land use estimates for the Holocene – HYDE 3.2. Earth System Science Data 9:927–953, doi:10.5194/essd-9-927-2017. Data: HYDE 3.2.1 baseline, DANS, doi:10.17026/dans-25g-gez3

layers.title: Pasture and grazing (modelled)
layers.note: Land grazed by livestock as a share of each cell: managed pasture and rough grazing (rangeland) together, from HYDE's country estimates spread by climate and population.

source.citation: Klein Goldewijk, K., Beusen, A., Doelman, J., Stehfest, E. (2017) Anthropogenic land use estimates for the Holocene – HYDE 3.2. Earth System Science Data 9:927–953, doi:10.5194/essd-9-927-2017. Data: HYDE 3.2.1 baseline, DANS, doi:10.17026/dans-25g-gez3

layers.title: Built-up area (modelled)
layers.note: Towns and other built-up land as a share of each cell, modelled by HYDE from its urban population estimates and typical town densities; compare the satellite built-up layer for 1975 and 2020.

source.citation: Klein Goldewijk, K., Beusen, A., Doelman, J., Stehfest, E. (2017) Anthropogenic land use estimates for the Holocene – HYDE 3.2. Earth System Science Data 9:927–953, doi:10.5194/essd-9-927-2017. Data: HYDE 3.2.1 baseline, DANS, doi:10.17026/dans-25g-gez3

layers.title: Bedrock geology (by period)
layers.note: The age of the solid rock under the soil, oldest in the north-west, youngest in the south-east. Carboniferous rocks hold the coal and much of the iron that fed the Industrial Revolution; Jurassic limestones gave Cotswold and Portland stone; Cretaceous chalk the downs. Irish age ranges spanning two periods are shown as the older one.

sources.citation: British Geological Survey (2025) BGS Geology 625k (DiGMapGB-625) bedrock, V5. Contains British Geological Survey materials © UKRI 2025

Geological Survey Ireland / Geological Survey of Northern Ireland (2024) Bedrock Geology 1:500,000 Ireland (ROI/NI). Contains Irish Public Sector Data (Geological Survey Ireland) licensed under CC BY 4.0; contains UK public sector information (GSNI) licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0

layers.title: Coalfields
layers.note: Areas over coal resources where planning consults the Coal Authority, a good outline of the British coalfields; mining towns grew on them from the 18th century.

sources.citation: Mining Remediation Authority (Coal Authority), Coalfield Consultation Areas. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0

layers.title: Railway stations open
layers.note: 9,282 railway stations with an opening year on Wikidata, from the first passenger lines of the 1820s. Closing dates are recorded for only 1,016 of them, so many stations closed in the 1950s–60s still show as open: the growth of the network is clearer than its contraction. Tram and metro stops are left out.

sources.citation: Wikidata contributors, railway stations (Q55488 and subclasses) with opening (P1619) and closing (P3999, P576) dates, queried 2026

layers.title: Railways and canals open
layers.note: 11,826 railway and 381 canal sections with an opening date on OpenHistoricalMap (from 1), drawn if open in the year shown. A volunteer map in progress: Scotland and northern England are well covered, Ireland and East Anglia thinly, so gaps are missing data, not missing lines.

sources.citation: OpenHistoricalMap contributors: railway, narrow-gauge and canal ways with start_date and end_date tags, queried 2026

layers.title: Ireland's counties: people compared with 1841
layers.note: Population of each of the 26 counties at each census from 1841, as a share of its 1841 figure: the Great Famine and a century of emigration halved most counties, and many in the west were still below half in 2022, while Dublin and its neighbours grew. The six counties of Northern Ireland are not in this table. Outlines are today's administrative counties.

sources.citation: Central Statistics Office, Ireland. FY001: Population at Each Census, 1841–2022, by county and sex

layers.title: Ice sheet and coast after the last Ice Age

legend.label: Land then, under the sea now
Ice in the largest estimate only

layers.note: The last British–Irish ice sheet from its greatest extent to its melting, and the coast as sea level rose and the land rebounded, every 1,000 years from 31,000 to 1,000 years ago. Ice outlines are the BRITICE-CHRONO best estimates from dated landforms (shaded paler where only their largest version has ice); land and sea come from their palaeotopographies (a model of the land's height above the sea of the time) compared with today's coast. Small glaciers after 15,000 years ago (the Loch Lomond Stadial) are not shown. Choose a date from the list: the year slider starts later.

sources.citation: Clark, C.D., Ely, J.C., Fabel, D., Bradley, S.L. (2022) BRITICE-CHRONO maps and GIS data of the last British-Irish Ice Sheet 31 to 15 ka, including model reconstruction, geochronometric age spreadsheet, palaeotopographies and coastline positions. PANGAEA, doi:10.1594/PANGAEA.945729; described in Clark et al. (2022) Growth and retreat of the last British-Irish Ice Sheet, 31 000 to 15 000 years before present. Boreas 51:699-758, doi:10.1111/bor.12594
NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (2022) ETOPO 2022 15 Arc-Second Global Relief Model, doi:10.25921/fd45-gt74 (30 arc-second version used for today's coast)

layers.title: Built-up land from satellites
layers.note: Share of the ground covered by buildings, mapped by the EU's Global Human Settlement Layer from Landsat and Sentinel-2 images, in cells of about 1 by 2 km. Shown for 1975 and 2020; before 1975 nothing is drawn.

sources.citation: Pesaresi, M. (2023) GHS-BUILT-S R2023A – GHS built-up surface grid, derived from Sentinel-2 composite and Landsat, multitemporal (1975–2030). European Commission, Joint Research Centre, doi:10.2905/9F06F36F-4B11-47EC-ABB0-4F8B7B1D72EA. © European Union, 1995–2025

layers.title: People per km² from satellites and censuses
layers.note: Census counts spread over the built-up areas seen by satellites (EU Global Human Settlement Layer), every five years from 1975 to 2020, in cells of about 1 by 2 km. Before 1975 nothing is drawn; for earlier centuries see the modelled people per km² (HYDE).

sources.citation: Schiavina, M., Freire, S., Carioli, A., MacManus, K. (2023) GHS-POP R2023A – GHS population grid multitemporal (1975–2030). European Commission, Joint Research Centre, doi:10.2905/2FF68A52-5B5B-4A22-8F40-C41DA8332CFE. © European Union, 1995–2025

layers.title: Lights at night from satellites
layers.note: How brightly the land shines at night, from the US military's DMSP satellites (1992–2013) and later VIIRS images converted to the same 0–63 scale (2014–2024), averaged over cells of about 1 by 2 km. Lit area grows with towns, roads and industry; the older sensor saturates in city centres, and the change of sensor can show as a step at 2014.

sources.short: Li et al. 2020, harmonised night-time lights
sources.citation: Li, X., Zhou, Y., Zhao, M., Zhao, X. (2020) A harmonized global nighttime light dataset 1992-2018. Scientific Data 7:168, doi:10.1038/s41597-020-0510-y; data version 10 (1992-2024), figshare doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.9828827.v10

layers.title: Tree cover lost since 2000
layers.note: Share of each cell (about 1.5 by 3 km) where satellites saw tree cover removed between 2001 and the year shown (Landsat, 30 m pixels). In Britain and Ireland most of it is plantation forestry felled for timber and later replanted, not permanent loss; regrowth is not shown.

sources.short: Hansen et al. 2013, Global Forest Change v1.12
sources.citation: Hansen, M.C., Potapov, P.V., Moore, R. et al. (2013) High-resolution global maps of 21st-century forest cover change. Science 342:850-853, doi:10.1126/science.1244693; data Global Forest Change 2000-2024 v1.12, University of Maryland

layers.title: Warmer or cooler than 1901–1930
layers.note: Average temperature of each decade compared with 1901–1930, in squares of half a degree (about 55 km), from weather-station records interpolated by the Climatic Research Unit. Grey is within 0.15 °C of the early-20th-century average.

sources.citation: Harris, I., Osborn, T.J., Jones, P., Lister, D. (2020) Version 4 of the CRU TS monthly high-resolution gridded multivariate climate dataset. Scientific Data 7:109, doi:10.1038/s41597-020-0453-3; data CRU TS v4.10, University of East Anglia Climatic Research Unit

layers.title: Wetter or drier than 1901–1930
layers.note: Average yearly rainfall of each decade as a share of 1901–1930, in squares of half a degree, from rain-gauge records interpolated by the Climatic Research Unit. Grey is within 4% of the early-20th-century average.

sources.citation: Harris, I., Osborn, T.J., Jones, P., Lister, D. (2020) Version 4 of the CRU TS monthly high-resolution gridded multivariate climate dataset. Scientific Data 7:109, doi:10.1038/s41597-020-0453-3; data CRU TS v4.10, University of East Anglia Climatic Research Unit

layers.title: Land cover (CORINE)
layers.note: What covers the land, from satellite images (patches of 25 hectares or more), with the 44 CORINE classes gathered into nine. Read from the EEA's generalised map at about 1.5 km; for exact areas use the full product. Before 2000 nothing is drawn.

sources.citation: Generated using European Union's Copernicus Land Monitoring Service information: CORINE Land Cover 2000, 2006, 2012 and 2018, doi:10.2909/960998c1-1870-4e82-8051-6485205ebbac (2018); read from the European Environment Agency's map service

layers.title: Tree cover from pollen
layers.note: Tree cover estimated from pollen in lake and bog cores with the REVEALS model, in squares of one degree, for time windows of a few centuries (the date shown is the middle of the window). Squares without enough pollen sites stay empty. Woodland spread after the Ice Age and was cleared by farmers from the Neolithic on.

sources.citation: Fyfe, R.M., Githumbi, E., Trondman, A.-K. et al. (2021) A full Holocene record of transient gridded vegetation cover in Europe. PANGAEA, doi:10.1594/PANGAEA.937075; described in Githumbi, E. et al. (2022) ESSD 14:1581–1619, doi:10.5194/essd-14-1581-2022

layers.title: Ancient woodland
layers.note: Share of each cell (about 1 by 2 km) that is ancient woodland: land wooded since at least 1600 in England and Wales and since about 1750 (Roy's Military Survey) in Scotland, from old maps; both surviving native woods and plantations on ancient woodland sites. Northern Ireland and Ireland are not included.

sources.citation: Natural England, Ancient Woodland (England). © Natural England copyright. Contains Ordnance Survey data © Crown copyright and database right 2026
© CNC/NRW, Ancient Woodland Inventory 2021; re-used under the Open Government Licence. Contains Ordnance Survey data
Copyright NatureScot. Contains Ordnance Survey data © Crown copyright and database right 2023

layers.title: Farmland quality (England)
layers.note: How good the land is for farming, graded from soil, climate, slope and wetness on the 1:250,000 provisional maps of the 1970s; not for single fields. England only.

sources.short: Provisional Agricultural Land Classification, Natural England
sources.citation: Natural England, Provisional Agricultural Land Classification (ALC) (England). © Natural England copyright. Contains Ordnance Survey data © Crown copyright and database right

layers.title: Superficial deposits (Great Britain)

legend.label: River alluvium, terraces and lake beds

layers.note: Loose deposits left on top of the bedrock, mostly by the ice ages: boulder clay, sands and gravels, river silts, peat and old beaches. Where none is shown the bedrock is at or near the surface. Great Britain only.

sources.citation: British Geological Survey (2025) BGS Geology 625k (DiGMapGB-625) superficial deposits, V5. Contains British Geological Survey materials © UKRI 2025

layers.title: Towns and cities by size
layers.note: Estimated population of the 192 places in Buringh's database of European cities that became sizeable towns (by century to 1500, every 50 years after); small towns that never grew are not in it. Dot area follows population; pale dots are Buringh's estimates where no figure survives. Positions are as given in the database.

sources.citation: Buringh, E. (2020) European urban population, 700–2000. DANS, doi:10.17026/DANS-XZY-U62Q; described in Buringh, E. (2021) Research Data Journal for the Humanities and Social Sciences 6(1):1–16, doi:10.1163/24523666-06010003

layers.title: Firms open
layers.note: 11,895 firms on Wikidata with a founding year and a position, coloured by industry. 10,928 are placed at their head office town, spread by up to a kilometre so they do not sit on one dot, so a dot is the firm's base, not its works. Closing years are recorded for only 2,371: many long-gone firms still show as open. The map keeps the firms that lasted or were written about, not every business of the time.

sources.citation: Wikidata contributors, companies (Q783794 and subclasses) and items directly of class business (Q4830453) or enterprise (Q6881511) in the isles or with their head office there, with founding (P571), dissolution (P576), coordinates (P625, else head office P159) and industry (P452), queried 2026 through QLever

layers.title: Boroughs by their first charter
layers.note: 258 towns with a charter (or other grant) dated before 1307 in British Borough Charters (Ballard 1913, Ballard and Tait 1923), 121 of them first after 1216, shown from the middle of the dated range of their earliest one: 57 mentioned as boroughs in Domesday Book, 122 founded by lesser lords, as the tables print them. A town appears with its earliest charter in the tables, not when it became a town or a borough. The charters to the Cinque Ports as a body, and Rathcool's (printed as in county Tipperary), are not placed.

sources.citation: Adolphus Ballard, British Borough Charters 1042-1216 (Cambridge University Press, 1913), Introduction section 4, Sources, pp. xxvi-xxxiii
Adolphus Ballard and James Tait, British Borough Charters 1216-1307 (Cambridge University Press, 1923), Introduction section 3, Sources, pp. xxv-xxxvi
